newsitem.title: USA: FIA offers alternative on U.S. CEA reform bill.
newsitem.headline: FIA offers alternative on U.S. CEA reform bill.

text.p: The Futures Industry Association, a large trade group, proposed Thursday a major alternative to a futures trading bill pending in the U.S. Senate -- creation of a vast "centralized professional trading market" with sharply reduced federal oversight.

The centralized market would be a consolidation of two proposals in the bill filed by Agriculture Committee leaders. One would allow professionals-only markets with a reduced level of control. The other would limit Commodity Futures Trading Commission oversight of foreign exchange trading to deals with retail customers if no other agency had control.
"FIA suggests that the committee consider consolidating these two provisions of the bill," FIA chairman Laurence Mollner said during a committee hearing.

Under the plan, the CFTC would have no jurisdication over transactions by participants unless they were executed on a designated contract market. CFTC would continue to regulate trading on commodity exchanges and retail-level deals.
Mollner argued the centralized market would reduce the confusion that would arise from the bill's two sections.
"Customers will not be able to understand why Treasury instruments and Eurodollars are treated differently," he said.
At the opening of the hearing, committee chairman Richard Lugar, Indiana Republican, said despite the variety of views on the bill, "I believe we are not as far from consensus as it might seem."
FIA members include the 70 largest futures brokerage firms.

The International Swaps and Derivatives Association, a trade group for commercial, merchant and investment banks, said it opposed the provision giving CFTC control of retail-level trading in foreign exchange. ISDA supported the overall bill in principle, however.
ISDA said the bill would guarantee more certainty that swaps transactions were exempt from CFTC regulation.

The National Futures Assocation, a regulatory body for the industry, said continued protection of small investors was important but it was appropriate to give a different level of regulation to sophisticated markets. NFA said it supported the bill's approach on the Treasury amendment.

The Managed Futures Association said the provision in the bill for a professionals-only market seemed a more restrictive version of the regulatory regime proposed on the Treasury amendment. It questioned if the professionals-only markets were needed when a more dynamic alternative was available.
